title: Information Timing and Release: The Gaming of Guidance!
gist: Damodaran links the SEC's proposal to replace quarterly reporting with semi-annual reporting and Kevin Warsh's push for less Fed guidance as two versions of the same question: does withdrawing information markets have learned to game make prices better or worse? His answer is that frequency is the wrong lever for corporate reporting (slim the reports, keep the quarters) but that the Fed genuinely should say less, because the data show fed funds rates follow market-set short rates rather than leading them and have only a 'meh' effect on real growth.

themes.theme: Two Information Withdrawals as One Debate

insights.claim: The SEC's floated move from quarterly to semi-annual corporate reporting and new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's push to give markets less forward guidance are structurally the same experiment: both remove a stream of 'news' markets have been using to calibrate prices.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: If both changes land, the informational cadence that drives quarterly repositioning and FOMC-date trading strategies changes at once; monitor both regulatory tracks as a single regime shift rather than separate stories.
insights.locator: The two stories may seem unconnected

insights.claim: The argument for less frequent corporate reporting (that it feeds market myopia) and the argument for less Fed guidance (that it creates trader gaming at the expense of fundamentals) are mirror images, and both face the identical pushback that removing information makes prices more volatile and less informative.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Frames the trade-off any investor should apply to disclosure-reduction proposals: less gaming versus wider price-discovery gaps and more scope for informed insiders.
insights.locator: The advocates for removing quarterly reports

themes.theme: Reporting Frequency: History and Global Reversals

insights.claim: US quarterly reporting is a recent regulatory artifact: the 1934 Securities Exchange Act mandated only annual 10-Ks, semi-annual reporting was added in 1955, and quarterly reports within 45 days of quarter-end only arrived in 1970.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'quarterly reporting is foundational' framing — a rollback would return the US to a regime it operated under for most of the SEC's existence.
insights.locator: The History of Earnings Reporting Periodicity

insights.claim: Frequent reporting was market-driven before it was mandated: the NYSE required most listed firms to report quarterly as early as 1939, and an estimated 60%+ of publicly traded companies were already disclosing quarterly in 1931, before either the SEC or NYSE required it.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Suggests dropping the mandate would not collapse disclosure — firms competing for investor capital chose transparency voluntarily even with no rule in place.
insights.locator: The first were the stock exchanges

insights.claim: Every major non-US market that adopted mandatory quarterly reporting this century has since reversed it: the UK imposed it in 2007 and allowed semi-annual again in 2014, the EU introduced it in 2007 and withdrew it in 2013, Singapore required it from 2003 for firms above S$20 million market cap then narrowed it in 2020, and Japan reversed its 2003 requirement in 2024.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A rich precedent set exists for studying what actually happened to volatility, liquidity and analyst coverage after quarterly reporting was withdrawn — the US would not be running a novel experiment.
insights.locator: The shift to more frequent reporting was slower

insights.claim: Emerging-market disclosure regimes diverge sharply, with India mandating quarterly financials (as do many Brazilian and Chinese companies) and Nigeria requiring quarterly, while South Africa and much of the rest of Africa run semi-annual mandates with voluntary quarterly releases.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Cross-border comparables carry unequal information density; models of EM companies on semi-annual reporting need wider estimation error bands than India- or China-listed peers.
insights.locator: In emerging markets, there are large variations

insights.claim: The early-2000s consensus that the rest of the world would converge on the US model of mandated quarterly reporting has failed, with the global drift running toward semi-annual mandates supplemented by voluntary quarterly disclosure of varying depth.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The SEC proposal is convergence with global practice rather than an outlier — raising the odds it eventually passes in some form.
insights.locator: In sum, the belief at the start of the twenty first century

themes.theme: Disclosure Diarrhea: Content Matters More Than Frequency

insights.claim: A typical US quarterly earnings report ran 2,000-5,000 words in 1980 and had tripled or quadrupled in size by 2000, with median word counts for Russell 3000 quarterly reports (2006-2020) and annual reports (1994-2020) still climbing.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Report length has grown far faster than report signal, which is the actual cost to investors — not the number of filings per year.
insights.locator: The Content of Earnings Reports

insights.claim: Four forces explain the bulking-up of earnings reports: accounting rule changes adding required disclosures, macro crises (visible as spikes in 2008/2009 and 2020) compounded by globalized exposure, legally defensive risk-exposure sections, and the rise of management guidance.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Gives a diagnostic for which parts of a filing to skip and which to read — only the accounting-rule-driven additions carry valuation content.
insights.locator: the bulking up of earnings reports can be explained

insights.claim: Damodaran labels the growth of filings 'disclosure diarrhea' and argues it has perversely reduced the information content of earnings reports rather than increasing it.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Argues the reform lever with actual investor value is trimming disclosure content, not cutting reporting frequency — a distinction most commentary conflates.
insights.quote: with more disclosure perversely making for less information
insights.locator: The bulking up of earnings reports is part of a phenomena

insights.claim: Damodaran says he has never found a company's risk-exposure disclosure section useful in a valuation because it is written by lawyers to provide legal cover rather than to inform.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Practical filing-reading rule: allocate research time to financial statements and footnotes, treat the risk-factor section as noise.
insights.quote: I have never found a risk disclosure useful in a valuation, as it seems to be written by lawyers with the objective of providing legal cover.
insights.locator: Legal Protection

insights.claim: Corporate earnings guidance is a product of the 1990s, enabled by the 1995 Safe Harbor Law and Reg FD, peaking in 2003 when more than 50% of companies issued guidance, and has since receded to roughly a fifth of firms.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Guidance withdrawal by individual companies is already the majority behavior, so a firm dropping guidance is far less of a red flag than markets often treat it.
insights.locator: Guidance

insights.claim: The earnings game runs on a specific pipeline: sell-side analysts publish EPS (and often revenue and margin) forecasts, services like Zacks, Google Finance and Yahoo! Finance aggregate them into quasi-public consensus estimates, forecasts are then revised in response to company news and macro developments, and the actual print is scored against that moving benchmark.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The tradable variable is the gap between the print and a consensus that itself moves — tracking revision trends is as informative as the final surprise.
insights.locator: The Earnings Game

insights.claim: Stock price responses sorted by earnings-surprise decile show the expected monotonic pattern (positive surprises up, negative down), but market reactions to earnings reports have become more muted over time, plausibly because analyst forecasts and revisions are now publicly accessible.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The historical earnings-surprise event edge is decaying as the input data commoditizes; strategies sized on older decile spreads will overestimate expected returns.
insights.locator: There is some evidence that the market responses

insights.claim: Post-earnings-announcement drift persists — positive surprises are followed by upward drifts and negative surprises by downward drifts in the days after release — and while the drift is small, Damodaran concedes it can still matter for active trading.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A residual, low-magnitude systematic edge for high-turnover strategies; not exploitable at long-horizon holding periods or high transaction costs.
insights.quote: While the price drift is small, it may still be large enough to make a difference in active trading, where winning by inches is still winning.
insights.locator: There is another aspect of the market reaction

insights.claim: Companies exploit the flexibility embedded in accounting rules to engineer beats of analyst estimates, with tech companies standing out, producing a disproportionately large share of positive earnings surprises across S&P 500 sectors in Q2 2026 per FactSet data.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A reported beat is weak evidence of operating outperformance — cross-check against cash flows and footnotes, especially in tech.
insights.locator: companies have learned to use the flexibility

insights.claim: Because routine beats are priced in, markets run on 'whispered earnings': a company with a history of coming in 5% or 10% above consensus is expected to keep doing so, and anything less is treated as a negative surprise despite being a nominal beat.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Model the firm's own historical beat magnitude as the real hurdle rate before positioning into a print — consensus is the wrong reference point.
insights.quote: investors build in the expectation that a company that has historically delivered earnings that are 5% or 10% above estimates will continue to do so, and a lesser number is a negative surprise
insights.locator: Second, as companies routinely beat analyst estimates

insights.claim: FactSet data on Q2 2026 S&P 500 reports show the link between earnings surprise and price reaction is now weak, with a significant subset of positive surprises producing price drops.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Trading the sign of the surprise is close to a coin flip in the current regime; the reaction function has decoupled from the headline beat.
insights.locator: As you can see, the linkage between earnings surprises

insights.claim: Damodaran wants the SEC to keep quarterly reporting frequency but slim the reports down, replacing one-size-fits-all disclosure requirements with targeted disclosures and refocusing filings on reporting what happened rather than prognosticating about the future.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The reform he would actually trade on is content-targeted disclosure; a frequency-only change leaves the underlying signal problem untouched.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: For an intrinsic-value investor the marginal impact of any single quarterly report on a company's value is small for many companies, but the price corrections around earnings dates act as catalysts that bring overvalued positions down and undervalued positions up.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The value of quarterly reporting to a long-term holder is realization timing, not valuation input — fewer reports means longer waits for mispricings to close.
insights.locator: I like quarterly reporting for two reasons

insights.claim: Damodaran says almost all the information he finds useful in an earnings report sits in the financial statements and footnotes, not in risk-exposure discussion or management guidance, and he would welcome eliminating those sections entirely.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Concrete prioritization for filing analysis: footnotes carry the valuation-relevant detail that headline numbers and MD&A narrative do not.
insights.locator: At the same time, almost all of the information

insights.claim: Damodaran deliberately excludes short-termism from his defense of quarterly reporting, arguing the term is undefined and self-serving — the cynical version being that any move against your position is short-term noise and any move in your favor is market wisdom.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Strips the main political rationale for the SEC proposal of analytical content, meaning the proposal's real effects should be judged on information and insider-access grounds instead.
insights.locator: Note that none of my arguments for preserving quarterly reporting

insights.claim: Damodaran argues that near-term profit-seeking is invariant across time and markets and cannot be regulated away, and that millions of opportunistic short-horizon trades are precisely what aggregates into a long-term rational price.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Policy attempts to lengthen investor horizons by throttling information should be expected to fail at their stated goal while imposing real information costs.
insights.quote: In fact, the magic of markets is that millions of trades motivated by opportunism and the short term can still yield a price that is long term and rational.
insights.locator: Second, I believe that most market participants

insights.claim: Short-term traders supply liquidity that long-term investors consume — a market of only fundamentals-driven long-term investors would be less liquid with higher transaction costs.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Any reform that suppresses short-horizon trading should be priced as a widening of the bid-ask spread borne by everyone, including buy-and-hold investors.
insights.locator: Finally, it remains true that if we were all long-term investors

insights.claim: Eliminating quarterly reports widens the window for insiders inside and outside the firm to trade profitably on material non-public information at the expense of public investors, even if that insider trading makes prices somewhat more informative.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The under-discussed cost of semi-annual reporting is a longer information asymmetry window — expect wider pre-announcement drift and more fairness complaints.
insights.locator: There is another issue that comes up in the context

insights.claim: Defenders of the status quo argue that removing quarterly reports would not end the earnings game but merely concentrate it, more intensively, into semi-annual reports.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Expect event-day volatility per report to rise if frequency falls — options positioning around fewer, larger catalysts becomes more valuable.
insights.locator: Those who are pushing for preserving the status quo

insights.claim: Damodaran predicts that if the SEC drops the quarterly mandate, many younger high-growth firms will voluntarily keep reporting quarterly — and those are exactly the companies where he would miss quarterly updates most because revenues and margins change quickly over short periods.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Screen for which growth names retain voluntary quarterly disclosure post-rule-change; those that quietly stop reporting quarterly deserve a higher discount for opacity.
insights.locator: I will miss the quarterly updates more with younger

insights.claim: Investors who began after 2008 credit the Fed almost entirely for low post-crisis rates and blame it for higher rates since 2022, a perception Damodaran calls both factually incorrect and unhealthy for how investors treat the Fed as savior or villain.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Portfolios built on Fed-reaction-function forecasting rest on an overstated causal premise; reweight toward inflation and growth forecasting instead.
insights.locator: Fed Guidance on Rates

insights.claim: Explicit Fed forward guidance is a post-2008 innovation — before the crisis the FOMC under Greenspan met eight times a year and sent only subtle hints, and the first explicit guidance was the 2008 signal that rates would stay low 'for some time', continued through Bernanke (2006-2014), Yellen (2014-2020) and Powell (2020-2026).
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Guidance is a ~18-year-old convention, not a structural feature of markets — its removal restores a regime that operated for decades.
insights.locator: The sea change in Fed behavior and centrality

insights.claim: Using monthly data on the effective fed funds rate, the 3-month Treasury bill and the 10-year Treasury note from January 1962 to June 2026, Damodaran finds fed funds rates are typically raised or cut after short-term Treasury rates have already moved, meaning the Fed mimics the market rather than leading it.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Trade the T-bill curve as the leading indicator and treat FOMC decisions as confirmation, not as the event that sets rates.
insights.quote: Fed funds rates tend to be increased (cut) after short term treasury rates have gone up (down), suggesting that the Fed is mimicking the market.
insights.locator: The Fed's Powers (and Powerlessness)

insights.claim: Breaking the 1962-2026 record into quarters where the fed funds rate rose, fell or was unchanged shows the bulk of the rate move happens before or during the quarter of the fed funds change, with only mild spillover into the following quarter for 3-month rates and almost none for long-term rates.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Positioning for a post-FOMC rate trend after a hike or cut has minimal historical basis, especially at the long end where duration risk actually sits.
insights.locator: At the bottom of the graph, I have a table

insights.claim: The link between fed funds rate changes and real GDP growth in the quarter before, of, and after the change (1962-2026 FRED data) is tenuous, with Volcker's hike to 20% in 1981 triggering a deep recession standing as an exception rather than the pattern.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Recession calls anchored on Fed tightening cycles have weak historical support; look to inflation and growth fundamentals for the real driver.
insights.quote: the fed effect on the real economy has been more "meh" than "wow"
insights.locator: The Fed's weaknesses in setting interest rates

insights.claim: Most of the variation in the 10-year US Treasury rate over time is explained by movements in inflation and real economic growth rather than by Fed action or inaction — an intrinsic risk-free rate framing.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Forecast the long rate as expected inflation plus expected real growth; that model beats trying to forecast the FOMC.
insights.locator: As you can see, much of the variation in long term interest rates

insights.claim: The Fed's genuine advantage is informational, not mechanical: through its twelve districts it collects data on price pressures and growth across the economy and has a bigger-picture view than any other government agency, so a fed funds change is best read as a signal of what the Fed sees in that data.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Treat FOMC moves as a read on the Fed's private economic dataset rather than as a lever on rates — the informational content survives even if the causal power does not.
insights.locator: To understand the extent and limits of the Fed's capacity

insights.claim: The rates that genuinely move with the fed funds rate are the narrow set directly tied to it — the prime rate and some credit card and CD rates — while the long-term market-set rates that drive asset valuation and matter most to borrowers show an even weaker relationship.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Consumer-credit-sensitive lenders have real fed funds beta; long-duration asset valuations do not, so don't cross-apply the transmission assumption.
insights.locator: Second, there are interest rates that are directly tied

insights.claim: The gap between perceived and actual Fed power is dangerous in two directions: it lets politicians pressure central banks to cut controlled rates into high inflation, which raises future inflation, and it diverts investor and business attention from the inflation fundamentals that actually drive rates and growth.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Political pressure for cuts amid 3% inflation is a tail risk to long-end yields and inflation expectations, not a bullish rates catalyst.
insights.locator: The gap between investor perception

themes.theme: The Warsh Doctrine and a Post-Guidance Market

insights.claim: Damodaran says politicians on both sides of the aisle believe Kevin Warsh can pull mortgage and Treasury rates down to 2% or lower at will, but with inflation expectations running at 2.5-3% there is no chance of that happening.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Fade positioning that anticipates a Warsh-driven collapse in long rates; the inflation-expectations floor caps how low yields can go regardless of Fed intent.
insights.quote: Warsh can bring rates (mortgage, treasury) down to 2% or lower, if he so desires, when the truth is that with inflation expectations running at 2.5-3%, there is no chance of that happening.
insights.locator: The Warsh Doctrine?

insights.claim: The FOMC left rates unchanged on July 29, 2026 with inflation running at 3% or more against a 2% target, and Damodaran reads the subtext as an acknowledgement that much of that inflation is being driven by a war and its effect on oil prices.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Supply-shock inflation is not rate-responsive, so the path of oil matters more to the Fed's next move than the domestic demand data.
insights.locator: In the context of today's (July 29, 2026) decision

insights.claim: Damodaran endorses reducing or withholding Fed guidance as a first step, but argues it must be paired with open humility from the Fed and Warsh about the limits of its powers and honesty about how often it follows markets rather than leading them.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Watch Fed communication for admissions of limited power — that rhetorical shift, more than the guidance cut itself, would signal a durable regime change in how rates are priced.
insights.quote: the end game should be a world where you see and hear from the Fed less, not more.
insights.locator: The pathway out of this problem will be long

insights.claim: Damodaran argues the surge in Fed guidance caused market participants to abdicate responsibility for judging fundamentals and gauging what interest rates should be, and that markets priced rates and stocks perfectly well before the guidance era began.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A post-guidance market should reward independent rate modeling and penalize consensus Fed-watching — an edge for managers with their own inflation and growth views.
insights.quote: the surge in guidance from the Fed has led many in markets to abdicate their responsibility for paying heed to fundamentals and gauging what interest rates should be.
insights.locator: There will be some who feel that markets will be lost

insights.claim: Damodaran's unifying conclusion is that there is nothing inherently good about more disclosure and that beyond a tipping point information overload causes investors to behave in perverse ways — applying equally to corporate filings and to FOMC commentary.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A general prior for evaluating any transparency proposal: measure marginal signal, not volume, and expect diminishing then negative returns to disclosure.
insights.quote: there is nothing inherently good about having more disclosure. In fact, there is a tipping point, where information overload can cause investors to behave in perverse ways.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Damodaran expects markets to step in and fill the informational vacuum left by reduced Fed guidance, which he argues benefits the Fed itself because its decisions are informed by those market judgments.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: If guidance is withdrawn, expect market-implied rate pricing (futures, bill curve) to become the primary signal and the FOMC to look increasingly reactive to it.
insights.locator: Markets will step in to fill the vacuum
